title: Review: Atom economy; Practical techniques and uncertainties; Covalent and dative bonding; Lewis structures
specRef: C1.3(k), C2.4(a), C2.4(b); C1.3(l), APP-C-1, APP-A(a); PRAC-PI5.2-1, PRAC-OA4-4, APP-A(c)-9, APP-A(a); ...
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD02#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM10#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM10#N.5, BD02#N.2, PR01a#N.12, PR01b#N.9, AM10#N.3, BD02#N.11, PR01a#N.5, AM10#N.9, BD02#N.12b, PR01a#N.10, PR01a#N.13. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Dative bond
items.clue: Formed when one atom supplies both shared electrons, as when H₂O joins H⁺.

items.label: Hazard
items.clue: Something that could cause harm, such as a corrosive or flammable substance.

items.label: Addition reaction
items.clue: Gives a single product, so 100% of the starting mass ends up in what is wanted.

items.label: Systematic error
items.clue: Shifts every reading the same way, e.g. heat lost to the air; repeats do not remove it.

questions.stem: Which reaction has an atom economy of 100% for the product named?

options.text: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), making calcium oxide
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l), making sodium sulfate
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), making sulfur trioxide
Any reaction that is carried out with a 100% yield

questions.explanation: This reaction has a single product, so every reactant atom ends up in it: 100%.

questions.stem: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?

options.text: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻

questions.explanation: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both. That attraction is the covalent bond.

questions.stem: A student plots the volume of gas collected against time. The line of best fit is straight, but does not pass through the origin. It passes through (10 s, 14 cm³) and (50 s, 62 cm³). What is the gradient, in cm³ s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: (62 − 14) ÷ (50 − 10) = 48 ÷ 40 = 1.2. The line meets the y-axis at 2 cm³, so one point alone gives the wrong answer.

questions.stem: A student must heat a reaction mixture containing ethanol (highly flammable, boiling point 78 °C) for 30 minutes. Which plan best controls the risk?

options.text: Heat it over a Bunsen burner on a low flame, in a fume cupboard.
Heat it over a Bunsen burner, wearing gloves and eye protection.
Heat it under reflux, using a water bath or an electric heater.
Heat it in an open beaker so that the vapour can escape.

questions.explanation: No naked flame, and the condenser returns ethanol vapour to the flask, so little escapes.

questions.stem: Which statement about atom economy and waste in an industrial process is correct?

options.text: The higher the percentage yield, the higher the atom economy, so less waste is produced.
Atom economy counts one molecule of each substance, so the coefficients do not affect it.
A process with an atom economy of 100% produces no waste of any kind at all.
The lower the atom economy, the greater the proportion of reactant mass that becomes waste.

questions.explanation: The mass not in the desired product ends up in by-products, so atom economy and waste are inversely related.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?

options.text: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen
The new bond formed from one electron supplied by nitrogen and one electron supplied by H⁺
All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen

questions.explanation: The new bond is co-ordinate: both electrons from N. Once formed, all four N–H bonds have the same length and strength.

questions.stem: A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. A student's titre is 12.50 cm³, found from two readings. What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?

Hydrogen is manufactured by reacting methane with steam: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). In one batch, 16.0 kg of methane gave 4.80 kg of hydrogen. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen by this reaction? (Aᵣ: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0)
questions.explanation: 3 × 2.0 ÷ (16.0 + 18.0) × 100 = 6.0 ÷ 34.0 × 100 = 17.6%. The products total is the same: 28.0 + 6.0 = 34.0. The rest of the mass ends up as CO.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide, CO, has 10 outer electrons, the same as N₂. Like N₂, it has a triple bond and one lone pair on each atom. Which describes the three shared pairs?

options.text: Three ordinary covalent bonds: C and O each supply three electrons.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from C to O.
Three co-ordinate bonds, all from O to C.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from O to C.

questions.explanation: C shares two electrons and O two: two ordinary pairs. O then donates one lone pair to C: C≡O with an arrow O→C. Each atom keeps one lone pair and has 8.

questions.stem: A student dissolves 2.5 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) in water and makes the solution up to 250.0 cm³. Which value of the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, is given to the appropriate number of significant figures?
questions.explanation: 2.5 ÷ 58.5 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.1709… The mass has only 2 significant figures, so the answer has 2: 0.17.

questions.stem: A student mixes two solutions in a polystyrene cup to find an enthalpy change. The thermometer has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C per reading, and the temperature rises by only about 4 °C. Which change would most reduce the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change, ΔT? -

options.text: Use larger volumes of the same two solutions.
Use more concentrated solutions, keeping the same volumes.
Start with both solutions at a higher temperature.
Record each temperature to two decimal places.

questions.explanation: More reacts in the same volume, so ΔT is larger (e.g. about 20 °C). The ±1.0 °C uncertainty in ΔT is then about 5% instead of 25%.
